steps.tx: A **posterior hip dislocation** accounts for nearly ninety percent of all traumatic hip dislocations. It represents an orthopaedic emergency resulting typically from dashboard trauma during high-speed frontal motor collisions. The patient flexed knee impacts the dashboard, transmitting immense axial force along the femoral shaft while the hip is flexed and adducted, violently driving the femoral head backwards.
steps.say: Posterior hip dislocation accounts for ninety percent of all hip dislocations. It is an emergency caused by dashboard trauma in car crashes. When the passenger flexed knee hits the dashboard, the axial force drives the femoral head out through the back of the hip socket.

vis.title: Hip Dislocation Patterns
rows: Dashboard impact with flexed and adducted hip

steps.tx: Bedside inspection reveals an unmistakable **characteristic limb attitude**. The affected lower limb rests fixed in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation with noticeable apparent limb shortening. The femoral head can often be palpated as an abnormal bony fullness in the gluteal region beneath the tensor fasciae latae, contrasting sharply with the flattened hollow overlying the femoral triangle.
steps.say: The bedside appearance is unmistakable. The injured leg is locked in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, with the knee resting against the opposite thigh. The limb looks shortened, and you can often feel the dislocated femoral head as a hard mass back in the gluteal region.

steps.tx: The primary neurological casualty is the **sciatic nerve**, injured in ten to twenty percent of posterior dislocations as the femoral head breaches the posterior capsule. The peroneal division is especially prone to traction contusion. Bedside examination reveals dropped foot with loss of ankle dorsiflexion, weak great toe extension, and anesthesia over the anterolateral lower leg and foot dorsum.
steps.say: Check sciatic nerve function immediately. The dislocated head can stretch or crush the sciatic nerve in up to twenty percent of patients. The common peroneal division suffers most, producing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and numbness over the top of the foot.

vis.title: Neurological Assessment in Posterior Dislocation
rows: Loss of ankle and toe dorsiflexion (foot drop)
Dorsum of foot and first web space
60 to 70 percent recover after prompt reduction
Loss of plantarflexion and toe flexion
Plantar aspect of foot and sole

steps.tx: Immediate **closed reduction** within six hours is imperative to salvage femoral head viability. Avascular necrosis incidence escalates from under five percent when reduced within six hours to over forty percent if reduction is delayed beyond twelve hours. The Allis technique employs supine inline axial traction with the hip and knee flexed ninety degrees while an assistant stabilizes the pelvis.
steps.say: Reduce the hip within six hours. The risk of avascular necrosis jumps from under five percent to over forty percent if you wait past six hours. In the Allis method, flex the hip and knee to ninety degrees with an assistant holding the pelvis, then pull the femur straight up toward the ceiling.

left.title: Allis Reduction Technique
points: Patient supine on floor or low table
Hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees
Smooth vertical upward traction on femur

right.title: Stimson Gravity Technique
points: Injured leg dangles over table edge

steps.tx: Following successful reduction, an immediate post-reduction **computed tomography** scan is mandatory. CT imaging rules out occult posterior acetabular rim wall fractures, loose intra-articular osteochondral fragments, and confirms concentric seating of the femoral head in the socket. If non-concentric reduction or intra-articular debris persists, urgent open arthrotomy is indicated to clear the joint space.
steps.say: Always get a CT scan right after reduction. Plain X-rays easily miss small cartilage fragments and posterior acetabular rim chips. A CT scan confirms that the joint space is completely symmetrical and that no loose bony fragments are grinding inside the joint.

vis.title: Post-Reduction CT Indications
rows: Open reduction and posterior wall screw plating
Pipkin Type I or II fracture
ORIF with headless screws or fragment excision

quiz.q: What is the classic clinical posture of the lower limb in a posterior hip dislocation?
options: Flexion, adduction, and internal rotation with shortening
Extension, abduction, and external rotation with lengthening
Flexion, abduction, and external rotation with shortening
Neutral extension, adduction, and external rotation
quiz.explain: A posterior hip dislocation classically presents with the affected limb held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation with apparent limb shortening.

quiz.q: Within what critical timeframe should a traumatic hip dislocation be reduced to minimize avascular necrosis?
quiz.explain: Closed reduction should be achieved within 6 hours. Delaying reduction beyond 6 hours causes prolonged kinking of retinacular vessels and sharply increases avascular necrosis risk from <5% to >40%.
